rationale: Isaiah 14 is the "song of contempt against the king of Babylon" (14:4, BSB), whose boast "I will ascend to the heavens" (14:13) is answered by "But you will be brought down to Sheol" (14:15). Matthew 11:23 has the same rise-and-fall shape: "will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!" In Greek the closing words match closely. Matthew's "heos hadou katabese" (Nestle 1904, Westcott-Hort) and the Septuagint's "eis haden katabese" at Isaiah 14:15 share the noun Hades and the same verb form, and differ in the preposition (and so in the noun's case). Two public-domain commentaries read via Bible Hub name the source: the Cambridge Bible ("The expressions recall Isaiah 14:13-15") and the Pulpit Commentary ("an adaptation of Isaiah's address to the King of Babylon"). The type is allusion because Matthew uses no citation formula and does not name Isaiah. The label is strong because the shared structure and the Greek wording can both be checked, and two named commentaries make the identification. It is not explicit, because the text itself does not point to Isaiah. Some later witnesses (the Byzantine text, followed by the KJV) read a statement ("which art exalted") instead of a question, with a different verb; the shared Hades phrase stands in both readings.
